cells.name: Performance art
cells.description: Work in which the artist is present and what they do is the material, made in front of an audience or recorded for one. It gathered as a named practice in the 1960s, and its terms are time, space, the body, the artist's presence, and the relation to the public. Usually only a photograph or a film is left afterwards, and how much of the work that carries is argued about inside the practice.

maps.explanation: A practice in the visual arts with its own literature, museums and canon since the 1960s.

questions: Fluxus, Gutai and Body Art are all made by doing something in front of people, and all three are left as roots or placed elsewhere; whether any of them sits under this cell needs a reading of their own sources.

cells.name: Information design
cells.description: Drawing made to explain something: a quantity, a network, an assembly, a route. The work is in choosing what to leave out, what to hold constant, and what the reader is meant to compare, so the drawing answers a question. Otto Neurath's pictorial statistics and Harry Beck's diagram of the London Underground are the cases it is taught from.

maps.explanation: A drawing practice with a canon and a taught method, holding the pictorial statistics and diagram cells.
Taught inside graphic design and applied to signage, timetables and instructions.

questions: Technical illustration is placed here because it draws to explain, though its home discipline is engineering documentation. The owner may prefer it as a root.

cells.name: Happenings
cells.description: Loosely scored events performed for a small audience, often in a non-art space, mixing action, objects, sound and the audience's own movement. Allan Kaprow used the word in 1959 and made the form a proposition about art that cannot be collected. Their documentation is partial by nature, which is part of their history.

maps.explanation: A named style or movement in the visual arts. The Artsy Art Genome lists it in its Styles and Movements family, and the references cited here confirm it.

broader.explanation: A happening is a performance, event or situation, usually as performance art.

cells.name: Viennese Actionism
cells.description: A short-lived Austrian movement of the 1960s and early 1970s in which Nitsch, Brus, Mühl and Schwarzkogler staged violent ritual actions using blood, animal carcasses and their own bodies. It works alongside performance, Fluxus and body art, and it goes further into taboo than any of them. Several actions were prosecuted, and the confrontation with Austrian post-war respectability was the point.

maps.explanation: A named style or movement in the visual arts. The Artsy Art Genome lists it in its Styles and Movements family, and the references cited here confirm it.

sources.title: Viennese Actionism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300047933

broader.explanation: Recorded on Wikidata as part of performance art, and placed among the 1960s efforts that developed performance, Fluxus, happening and body art.

cells.name: Isotype
cells.description: The picture language developed by Otto Neurath and Gerd Arntz from the 1920s for showing social and economic facts. Quantity is shown by repeating a countable pictogram rather than by scaling one, the symbols are cut to a fixed geometric grammar, and colour and layout are ruled by the comparison being made.

maps.explanation: A designed symbol system with a documented body of published charts.
It is the origin of the modern pictogram set, and design languages take their symbol grammar from it.

broader.explanation: Neurath and Arntz built the picture language to show social and economic facts under a fixed grammar, which is what this practice does.

questions: Getty AAT has no concept for Isotype; the cell cites Wikipedia and Wikidata.

cells.name: Transit map
cells.description: The diagram of a transport network drawn for a rider. Geography is abandoned, lines run at fixed angles, stations are spaced evenly, and interchanges get a symbol of their own, so the drawing preserves only the order of stops and where lines meet.

maps.explanation: A diagrammatic tradition with a documented history and a large published body of work.
It is an information design practice, and design languages take its line grammar and node conventions from it.

broader.explanation: The diagram drops geography to preserve the order of stops and the interchanges, so it is drawn around the rider's question.

questions: Getty AAT has no concept for this; the cell cites Wikipedia and Wikidata.

cells.name: Technical illustration
cells.description: Drawing a made object so that someone can build, service or understand it. Views are orthographic or axonometric, line weight shows the hierarchy, parts are pulled apart along their assembly axes, and callouts and section cuts label the parts and open the interior. Patent drawings, service manuals and cutaways are its published body of work.

maps.explanation: An illustrative tradition with conventions of its own and a large published body of work.
Design languages take its line hierarchy, callout grammar and drafting conventions from it.

broader.explanation: The drawing is built so someone can assemble, service or understand the object, which is the explanatory purpose this practice is defined by.
